 20 Most Universally Loved K-Dramas, Ranked

 By  
 Shealyn Scott 
 Published Nov 20, 2026, 11:30 AM EST 
 Shealyn Scott is a Senior Writer at Screen Rant. She has been writing for the site since 2024, focused on network, reality, streaming, and classic television.
A creative writer, journalist, and lover of the written word in all its forms, Shealyn enjoys deconstructing scenes from her favorite shows, using context clues and historical precedent to predict major plot points (which, due to her successful track record, has sparked rumors of clairvoyance).
As an award-winning student journalist, Shealyn spent her college years advocating for the humanities while studying English Literature. Her love of storytelling propelled her to expand her degree with minors in Writing and History, believing life to be a mere collection of stories that can be framed in as many ways as a movie scene.
As a Senior member of the TV Team, Shealyn treats the series she covers like books, analyzing every line, camera angle, and lighting choice. Thankfully, her personal mission statement lines up perfectly with Screen Rant: every creative work deserves just as much thought from the viewer as it received from its creator.

 The K-drama world has changed dramatically in recent years, but there are plenty of beloved titles that are sure to stand the test of time. There are more eyes on the genre than ever before, meaning the industry itself is constantly evolving. As a result, arduous craft and creativity have produced K-drama masterpieces that define the age of streaming.

 From familiar K-dramas that have aged like fine wine to fresh, boundary-pushing series, the genre landscape is irrefutably flourishing. On one hand, innovation runs wild and rising stars are making names for themselves. At the other end of the spectrum, established actors are expanding their prolific filmographies with modern classics. Whether you prefer the tropes of first-gen favorites or the artistry of streaming-era standouts, however, K-drama fans are spoiled for choice.
 20 
 Guardian: The Lonely and Great God
 Kim Byung-chul as Park Joong-heon in Goblin/Guardian: The Lonely and Great God. 
 Throughout the decade since its release, Guardian: The Lonely and Great God (also known as Goblin ) has remained a classic K-drama that many consider a must-watch. The eponymous Kim Shin (Gong Yoo) is a delightfully disillusioned Dokkaebi (goblin) whose immortality feels more like a prison than a power.
 There's a fairly formulaic love story between Kim Shin and the Goblin Bride from his divine prophecy, but Guardian: The Lonely and Great God shines when it explores the dynamics within its ensemble. From an endearing Grim Reaper (Lee Dong-wook) to a vengeful spirit, the side characters are what truly keep the 2016 K-drama in the conversation. The central romance isn't as timeless, but the sheer gravitas makes the fantasy drama a fan-favorite.
 19 
 Her Private Life
 Ryan Gold and Sung Duk-mi in Her Private Life. 
 Similarly, Park Min-young is one of the biggest stars in K-drama history, and her mere existence gives a series staying power. Many of her best are office romance K-drama , including What's Wrong with Secretary Kim, Marry My Husband, and her magnum opus: Her Private Life. 
 In the 2019 rom-com, Park brings protagonist Sung Deok-mi to life with immeasurable care. An art curator by day and superfan by night could have been a flat, cliché character, but Park Min-young keeps the main character dynamic enough to enthrall viewers. Between her impeccable acting and the captivating romance with Kim Jae-wook's Ryan Gold, Her Private Life maintains a cult following over seven years later.​​​​​​
 18 
 Reply 1988
 The cast of Reply 1988. 
 The Reply anthology is an unforgettable feat of storytelling, but Reply 1988 is its most impressive installment by far. The coming-of-age drama follows five childhood friends dealing with growing pains, familial drama, and the effects of major global events.
 Reply 1988 balances its dual timelines well, revealing early on that the female lead's future husband is within the friend group. Beyond turning the series into a relatable K-drama about first love , the subplot adds an element of mystery that runs as a comforting underlying current. Over a decade after its debut, there are few dramas as nostalgic as Reply 1988.​​​​​​ 
 17 
 My Mister
 Lee Ji-an (Lee Ji-eun/IU) in My Mister. 
 There are countless K-pop idols who take a stab at acting, but IU's K-dramas are a cut above the rest. Although the pop star has been acting since 2011, My Mister was the breakout role that legitimized her acting career in the eyes of millions. As Lee Ji-an, IU is the emotional centerpiece of My Mister, portraying an extremely complex character who transforms from victim to perpetrator to victim once more. 
 Rather than amp up high-octane fight scenes or add in a romantic twist, My Mister allows its psychological drama to take center stage, drawing out its narrative with understated confrontations and seemingly innocuous details that build up to a tragic crescendo. Admittedly, it isn't the easiest watch, but there's no denying the positive impact My Mister has had on IU's career.​​​​​​
 16 
 Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha
 Close Shin Min-a and Kim Seon-ho in Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha 
 Kim Seon-ho and Shin Min-a in the K-drama Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha. 
 Shin Min-a and Kim Seon-ho in Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha 
 When Yoon Hye-jin (Shin Min-a) uproots her metropolitan life to open a dental clinic in a seaside town, she finds herself inexplicably drawn to Hong Du-sik (Kim Seon-ho), an honorary village chief who wanders like a nomad to help anyone in need. With their palpable chemistry and opposites-attract appeal, Yoon Hye-jin and Hong Du-sik are one of the most iconic K-drama couples in recent memory.
 Truthfully, Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha is near-perfect as a romance series. It packs a surprisingly emotional punch with the male lead's devastating backstory and an eleventh hour bombshell. Nevertheless, the 2021 series is confined to rom-com rules, meaning bids for affection and established relationship conflicts can feel a tad cliché. Regardless, Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha is the definition of a comfort watch.​​​​​​
 15 
 Lovely Runner
 Byeon Woo-seok as Ryu Sun-jae and Kim Hye-yoon as Im Sol in Lovely Runner. 
 Likewise, Lovely Runner took the framework of a coming-of-age romance and raised the stakes with magical time-slips and a looming murder mystery. In the current timeline, Ryu Sun-jae (Byeon Woo-seok) is a famous idol who seems fated to suffer an untimely death. To save her favorite star, Im Sol (Kim Hye-yoon) travels back to 2008, where she discovers her K-pop bias was actually her secret admirer in high school.

 ​​​​​​Unsurprisingly, the K-drama was an instant success, with it deservedly lauded as an amalgam of the best traits of each of its sub-genres. From Lovely Runner 's time travel fantasy to its heartwarming central romance, the drama is a perfect fit for anyone who loves a good "right person, wrong time" story.
 14 
 Hospital Playlist
 The five main characters of Hospital Playlist. 
 The vast majority of modern K-dramas are one-season wonders, but Hospital Playlist exceeded expectations with a 24-episode, two-season run. The medical drama follows a group of doctors at the central Yulje Medical Centre, each of whom offers a different perspective via their given specialty (ranging from pediatrics to neurosurgery).
 Hospital Playlist is one of the most bingeable K-dramas on Netflix , largely thanks to its sprawling worldbuilding and extensive cast. Despite the size of the ensemble, each character feels true to life and fully lived in, which only bolsters the medical drama's realism.
 13 
 Vincenzo
 Credit: MovieStillsDB 
 Vincenzo is genuinely a one-of-a-kind series, as it fuses the familiar archetypes of a Korean drama with the violence of a classic mafia movie. Without question, Vincenzo 's mob drama is the foundation of its premise and what may initially hook viewers, but there's a fascinating conversation of morality running alongside the main plot that keeps the audience spellbound.
 As the title suggests, Vincenzo Cassano (Song Joong-ki) is the main character, though he's far more of an antihero than a traditional protagonist. Before the record-breaking release of Squid Game changed the genre forever, Vincenzo 's brutal torture scenes put it in a league of its own, and the dark comedy is still worth a weekend binge.​​​​​​​
 12 
 Signal
 A man and woman stare at each other in a police station in the K-drama Signal. 
 There are dozens of K-dramas that incorporate fantasy elements for romance, mystery, or both, but Signal is the prototypical time-travel crime drama. After profiler Park Hae-young (Lee Je-hoon) discovers an abandoned walkie-talkie, he miraculously gets in contact with Jae-han (Cho Jin-woong), a detective who has been missing for 15 years.
 From the past, the presumed dead detective helps Hae-young and Detective Cha Soo-hyun (Kim Hye-soo) solve cold cases. All the while, the truth behind Jae-han's disappearance continues to be the toughest case for the trio to solve. Though there are certainly aspects that age the series, Signal is a defining K-drama thriller that genre fans shouldn't overlook.​​​​​​​
 11 
 The Glory
 Anyone remotely interested in K-dramas in the early 2020s knows about The Glory . The quintessential revenge K-drama follows Moon Dong-eun (Song Hye-kyo), a woman who devises a plan to get back at her high school bullies as adults. Unlike most American dramas— where bullying is commonly limited to online attacks or small in-person confrontations— The Glory paints a harrowing picture of South Korean school violence, and Dong-eun has the curling iron burns to prove it.
 As awful as it is to watch a young girl be tormented by bored rich kids, each antagonist is meticulously crafted, and their inevitable downfall plays out like a wildly satisfying domino effect. Of course, The Glory is far more than a simple revenge fantasy, and some of the most gratifying moments hit when you least expect them.​​​​​​
